title: The Most Equally Distributed
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Discourse on the Method by René Descartes, translated by John Veitch (Project Gutenberg edition).
body: Good sense is, of all things among men, the most equally distributed; for every one thinks himself so abundantly provided with it, that those even who are the most difficult to satisfy in everything else, do not usually desire a larger measure of this quality than they already possess. And in this it is not likely that all are mistaken; the conviction is rather to be held as testifying that the power of judging aright and of distinguishing truth from error, which is properly what is called good sense or reason, is by nature equal in all men; and that the diversity of our opinions, consequently, does not arise from some being endowed with a larger share of reason than others, but solely from this, that we conduct our thoughts along different ways, and do not fix our attention on the same objects.

For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it. The greatest minds, as they are capable of the highest excellences, are open likewise to the greatest aberrations; and those who travel very slowly may yet make far greater progress, provided they keep always to the straight road, than those who, while they run, forsake it.

For myself, I have never fancied my mind to be in any respect more perfect than those of the generality; on the contrary, I have often wished that I were equal to some others in promptitude of thought, or in clearness and distinctness of imagination, or in fullness and readiness of memory. And besides these, I know of no other qualities that contribute to the perfection of the mind.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the author say is "of all things among men, the most equally distributed"?
options: Good sense
Wealth
Physical strength
Memory

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author say is "properly what is called good sense or reason"?
options: The power of judging aright and of distinguishing truth from error
The ability to memorize large amounts of information
The capacity to speak persuasively in public
The skill of solving mathematical equations quickly

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the author say actually causes the diversity of people's opinions?
options: Conducting thoughts along different ways and not fixing attention on the same objects
Some people having a larger share of reason than others
Differences in education and upbringing alone
Differences in physical strength and stamina

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author say is "the prime requisite" beyond simply possessing a vigorous mind?
options: Rightly to apply it
Sharing it generously with others
Testing it against the opinions of philosophers
Writing it down in a book

questions.prompt: According to the passage, to what are "the greatest minds" also said to be open?
options: The greatest aberrations
The greatest honors
The greatest wealth
The greatest friendships

questions.prompt: Per the passage, in what three qualities does the author say he wished he were equal to others?
options: Promptitude of thought, clearness of imagination, and readiness of memory
Physical strength, wealth, and social standing
Skill in mathematics, music, and painting
Courage, patience, and generosity

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say that those who "travel very slowly" may make "far greater progress" than those who run?
options: Steady, careful reasoning along a correct method matters more than raw quickness of mind
Slow travelers are simply more physically fit than fast ones
Speed is always harmful and should be avoided in any task
Running causes people to become lost more easily than walking

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say it is "not likely that all are mistaken" in believing they have enough good sense?
options: Such near-universal agreement suggests good sense really is distributed equally by nature, rather than being a shared illusion
Most people have carefully studied philosophy and tested their own reasoning
Everyone has been told the same thing by their teachers
The author has personally surveyed every person he has met

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Reason is equally shared by all people, so what matters most is applying it correctly and steadily rather than possessing an exceptional natural mind
Only a rare few people are born with the capacity for good judgment
The author believes his own mind is far superior to that of ordinary people
Progress in thinking depends entirely on natural talent rather than method

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the greatest minds are open to the greatest "aberrations"?
options: Errors or deviations from what is correct
Achievements and honors
Friendships and alliances
Physical illnesses

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who does the author say usually does not desire a larger measure of good sense?
options: Even those who are the most difficult to satisfy in everything else
Only the wealthiest members of society
Only trained philosophers
Only those who have studied at a university

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author say is "not enough" on its own?
options: Possessing a vigorous mind
Owning many books
Having many friends
Living a long life

questions.prompt: According to the passage, does the author claim that his own mind is more perfect than other people's?
options: No, he says he never fancied it more perfect than those of the generality
Yes, he claims to be far more intelligent than most
He claims only his memory is superior to others'
He claims only his imagination is superior to others'

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author say he knows of no other qualities besides those three that contribute to?
options: The perfection of the mind
The wealth of a nation
The happiness of a family
The strength of an army

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the author list specific qualities like memory and imagination when denying that his mind is exceptional?
options: To show humility while still suggesting that his careful method, not natural gifts, is the source of his achievements
To prove that he has no useful mental qualities at all
To argue that memory and imagination are unimportant qualities
To boast that he possesses all of these qualities in abundance

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the passage's argument about reason and progress?
options: Since reason is shared equally by all, real progress comes from applying it correctly and steadily rather than from raw natural talent
Progress depends entirely on being born with an exceptional mind
Only the fastest thinkers ever make meaningful progress
Reason varies greatly from person to person by nature

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does "promptitude of thought" mean?
options: Quickness or speed of thinking
Careful, slow deliberation
Forgetfulness or absent-mindedness
Confusion about a topic
